content: Exposure to sexual contact and the potential underreporting of both injecting and non-injecting recreational drug use are significant factors in the transmission of hepatitis B and C. Healthcare workers are particularly at risk for occupational transmission of viral hepatitis, primarily through percutaneous injuries involving needles during vascular access procedures. Transmission can also occur via contact with blood and body fluids on skin lesions or mucous membranes. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), several factors contribute to a higher risk of occupational acquisition of hepatitis. These include working with populations with a higher prevalence of infection, higher rates of unnecessary injections in healthcare settings, the use of unsterilized needles and equipment without needle-stick safety mechanisms, inadequate implementation of standard precautions, and insufficient coverage of hepatitis B vaccination. Certain populations, such as patients with thalassemia or hemophilia who require multiple transfusions, and those undergoing hemodialysis, are at increased risk of hepatitis B and C due to repeated exposure to blood products. Invasive procedures, including cosmetic practices like tattooing and body piercing, as well as traditional medicine practices such as scarification and circumcision, also carry a small but increased risk of hepatitis B and C transmission, particularly when contaminated equipment is used. Individuals living with HIV are at a higher risk of hepatitis C infection. In regions with high prevalence rates of hepatitis B and C, children exposed to HIV through mother-to-child transmission are also at increased risk of acquiring these infections. Perinatal or early childhood transmission is the predominant route of hepatitis B infection in many parts of the world, especially in endemic regions, where up to 90% of chronic hepatitis B infections are attributable to mother-to-child transmission. The risk of hepatitis C transmission during the perinatal period is estimated to be 4–8%, increasing to 10–25% among children born to mothers co-infected with HIV. Globally, approximately 2 billion people show evidence of past or present hepatitis B infection, with 248 million being chronic carriers of the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). The prevalence of HBsAg varies significantly by geographical region, with the highest rates (>5%) observed in sub-Saharan Africa, East Asia, parts of the Balkans, the Pacific Islands, and the Amazon Basin. In contrast, regions such as Central America, North America, and Western Europe have a prevalence below 2%. Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is a major cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), with an estimated 686,000 deaths annually attributed to these complications. Horizontal transmission, including household and child-to-child transmission, is an important route of hepatitis B infection, particularly in children. Up to 50% of childhood CHB cases cannot be explained by mother-to-child transmission. However, horizontal transmission does not appear to play a significant role in hepatitis C transmission among children. Adolescents who missed hepatitis B vaccination during infancy or early childhood are at risk of infection. While the risk of sexual transmission of hepatitis C is generally low, it is slightly increased among individuals with multiple sexual partners. Vulnerable adolescents, such as those who inject drugs or engage in sex work, are at higher risk of hepatitis B and C infection. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is an enveloped DNA virus belonging to the Hepadnaviridae family. It causes both acute and chronic infections, ranging from asymptomatic cases to severe or fulminant hepatitis. Chronic hepatitis B is defined as the persistence of HBsAg in the blood for more than six months, with or without active viral replication and evidence of liver injury or inflammation. The risk of chronic infection is highest in neonates (90% of those born to HBeAg-positive mothers) and young children under five years of age (20–60%), but it is less common in adults (<5%). The natural history of CHB is dynamic and progresses through several non-linear phases, which vary in duration and do not always align with criteria for antiviral therapy. Key serological markers, such as HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBc, and HBV DNA, are used to differentiate acute from chronic infection, stage the disease, and guide treatment decisions. HBsAg is the first serological marker to appear, followed by HBeAg, which indicates high levels of viral replication. In acute infections that resolve, HBeAg seroconverts to anti-HBe, and HBsAg disappears. In chronic infections, HBeAg may persist, or seroconversion may be delayed. Vaccination is the most effective strategy for preventing hepatitis B infection. Administering the hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth, followed by at least two additional doses, is 90–95% effective in preventing infection and reducing transmission. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends universal hepatitis B vaccination for all infants, with the first dose given as soon as possible after birth.
